# contextd

> Continuous context manager for AI coding agents. It watches an agent's session from outside,
> keeps a structured persistent record of the project (goals, decisions, constraints, discoveries,
> open issues, important files) and serves back only the part that is relevant. The agent's context
> is disposable; the project's state is persistent. Local-first: state lives in the project's
> `.context/` directory (SQLite); nothing leaves the machine unless you configure a remote model.

Works with Claude Code (hooks + MCP) and Codex (rollout files + MCP). Node 22+.

## If you were asked to set contextd up

```bash
git clone https://github.com/Fabri45555/context-master.git && cd context-master
npm install && npm run build && npm link    # puts `contextd` on PATH

cd <the user's project>
contextd init --mcp                         # config, Claude Code hooks, MCP registration
contextd doctor                             # every check should pass before relying on it
contextd ui                                 # optional: the dashboard on localhost
```

The MCP server is loaded when an agent session starts: register it, then start a new session.
For an agent with no hooks and no MCP, `contextd mirror --target agents` writes the memory into
AGENTS.md. `contextd import --from claude-memory` brings in Claude Code's own memory files.
`contextd uninstall` removes only what contextd added.

## If you are an agent in a project that uses contextd

- Start of a session: call `memory_bootstrap` before reading files. It returns the current task,
  active constraints, decisions and open issues in a few hundred tokens.
- Before working on an area: `memory_query` with what you are about to do.
- When a decision, constraint or costly discovery is settled: `memory_remember`.
- When the task changes or finishes: `memory_task`. When a goal is met: `memory_close`.
- `memory_explain` says why an item exists; `memory_conflicts` finds contradictions;
  `memory_retire` removes what is wrong.
- The repository is the source of truth for code. Memory holds intent, never file contents.
